catalog_quote: [p. 131, on Bada and Leboni] Ten opzichte van den klemtoon valt op te merken, dat de laatste lettergreep van een zin steeds met opgang der stem, dus met rijzenden klemtoon, wordt uitgesproken. In het Badasch en in het Lebonisch trof het ons ook dat de losse woorden die men ons noemde, steeds met ascendent rythme werden gezegd. Het woord maroa (goed) werd dan uitgesproken marwá; bij sommigen klonk het als mar'á. In een zin echter waar maroa niet het laatste woord is, valt de klemtoon op ro. Overigens is de klemtoon als in het Napoesch. [p. 119, on Napu] Éénlettergrepige suffixen bewegen den klemtoon ééne plaats naar achteren. In het Bare'e is dit niet het geval. Het Napoesch zegt: anoengkoe (van mij), met den klemtoon op noe, het Bare'e anoekoe, klemtoon op a. [p. 138, on Leboni] Over den klemtoon is alleen dit te zeggen, dat hij steeds valt op de voorlaatste lettergreep. De achtervoegsels bewegen dus den klemtoon evenveel plaatsen naar achteren, als zij lettergrepen tellen. Encliticae laten den klemtoon onbewogen. [p. 462, on Bare'e] Daar de klemtoon in het algemeen op de voorlaatste lettergreep valt, vormt ieder grondwoord rythmisch een trochee.

new_statements.translation: As regards stress it should be noted that the last syllable of a sentence is always pronounced with a rise of the voice, i.e. with rising accent. In Bada and in Leboni we also found that the isolated words that were given to us were always said with ascending rhythm. The word maroa 'good' was then pronounced marwá; with some it sounded like mar'á. In a sentence, however, where maroa is not the last word, the stress falls on ro. Otherwise the stress is as in Napu. [p. 131] — Monosyllabic suffixes move the stress one place to the right. In Bare'e this is not the case. Napu says anoengkoe 'of me' with the stress on noe, Bare'e anoekoe with the stress on a. [p. 119, Napu]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Bada is penultimate, as in Napu (and Bare'e, where the authors state that stress in general falls on the penultimate syllable, p. 462); in Napu, and hence Bada, monosyllabic suffixes shift the stress one syllable rightward so that it stays on the penult of the suffixed word (anoeng-koe stressed on noe). The last syllable of a sentence carries a rising intonation, which in citation-form elicitation made isolated Bada words sound final-accented (maroa -> marwá); in non-final position the same word is stressed on the penult (ro).
new_statements.exceptions: Utterance-final rising pitch on the last syllable of a sentence; isolated (citation) words elicited with 'ascending rhythm', i.e. apparent final prominence, which the authors treat as a phrase-final intonation effect rather than word stress. Enclitics are said (for Leboni, p. 133) to leave the stress unmoved, while suffixes move it.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement is indirect ('as in Napu') and is embedded in a comparative sketch of Bada/Besoa vs Napu from fieldwork of the 1900s-1910s; the explicit sentences concern citation forms versus words inside a sentence (phrase-level rising pitch on the final syllable of the sentence). No modern instrumental or phonological description of Bada stress was found.
new_statements.identity_note: Adriani & Kruijt 1914 describe 'het Badasch' (Bada proper, the ti'ara language of the Bada plateau, ~5000 speakers) and treat Besoa [bep] as a dialect of the same language, giving only Besoa differences; the stress paragraph names Bada and Leboni (Rampi-Leboni [lje]) explicitly and refers to Napu [npy] for the rest. Martens 1989 (Badaic = Bada, Besoa, Napu) confirms the grouping but says nothing about stress.

sources.note: p. 131 (scan p. 145, verified on the page scan): sentence-final syllable always pronounced with rising voice; isolated Bada words elicited with ascending rhythm (maroa 'good' -> marwá / mar'á), but in non-final position stress falls on ro (penult); 'otherwise the stress is as in Napu'.
